learningObjective: Distinguish end-to-end model speedup from kernel-level speedup when interpreting the PyTorch 2 paper's `torch.compile` results.

canonicalClaims.claim: The PyTorch 2 paper's headline speedups (e.g. geomean speedup on the TorchBench-style suites) are end-to-end model speedups measured against eager execution on the same hardware; individual kernels inside those runs can be much faster or much slower, and kernel-level speedups from generated Triton kernels cannot be reported as end-to-end speedups without accounting for graph breaks, launch overhead, host-side work, and non-compiled parts of the program.
conditions: The comparison baseline is eager PyTorch on the same hardware and PyTorch version.
The workload includes host-side Python overhead, data-loading and possibly graph breaks.
nonImplications: Does not imply that a kernel improvement always yields the same end-to-end improvement; Amdahl's law limits the benefit.
Does not imply the reported numbers hold for arbitrary models; they are conditioned on the paper's benchmark suite.

sourceMappings.locator: § evaluation methodology and reported end-to-end speedups

misconceptions.claim: If TorchInductor's generated Triton attention kernel is 3× faster than the eager attention kernel, the whole model runs ~3× faster under `torch.compile`.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Amdahl's law: end-to-end speedup depends on the fraction of runtime spent in that kernel and on non-accelerated portions (host-side code, non-compiled subgraphs). Kernel-level speedup rarely equals end-to-end speedup.

misconceptions.claim: `torch.compile` end-to-end speedups over eager are hardware-independent; a paper's numbers on A100 apply directly to any GPU.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Kernel choice, memory-bandwidth ratios, Tensor Core precision availability and compile time all depend on hardware; the paper's numbers are conditioned on the specific evaluation setup.

misconceptions.claim: The paper's reported speedups include compile time in the total, so 'end-to-end' means 'compile + inference' latency.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The PyTorch 2 paper distinguishes compile-time and steady-state throughput; headline speedups are typically steady-state after warm-up, and compile time is reported separately.
